verdict.summary: unix_getpw dereferences encrypted_pass at `if (encrypted_pass[0] == 0)` without any NULL check on the paths reaching it. encrypted_pass is assigned from getpwnam()->pw_passwd (or getspnam()->sp_pwdp), i.e., pointers parsed from external passwd/shadow/NSS data for the attacker-chosen User-Name. The only NULL test, `if ((encrypted_pass == NULL) || (strlen(encrypted_pass) < 10))`, exists only under #ifdef HAVE_GETSPNAM, does not reject anything, and merely replaces one possibly-NULL pointer with another unchecked one (`encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp;`). On builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM there is no check at all. A record with a NULL password field — the exact case the code's own `encrypted_pass == NULL` test anticipates — flows straight to the dereference, crashing the authentication handler: an attacker-reachable denial of service (CWE-476).

evidence.reason: Sink: encrypted_pass is dereferenced (`encrypted_pass[0]`) and consumed as a string by pairmake with no NULL guard on any path. Any User-Name whose passwd/shadow record returns a NULL password pointer reaches this line and crashes the process.

Origin/partial guard: the only NULL test in the function proves the authors treat encrypted_pass as possibly NULL, yet it neither rejects the request nor validates the replacement value spwd->sp_pwdp; after this block encrypted_pass may still be NULL at the line-137 dereference, and on builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM the assignment at line 46 (`encrypted_pass = pwd->pw_passwd;`) has no check at all.

assumptions: request->username->vp_strvalue is assumed NUL-terminated by the attribute decoder; no statement in this code establishes termination or length of name.

pairmove(vp_list, &vp) is assumed to leave vp pointing only at pairs not moved into vp_list, so pairfree(&vp) frees the remainder; the contract of pairmove is not shown, so a double-free cannot be confirmed or excluded from this code alone.
radlog/radlog_request are assumed not to fail in a way that affects control flow; their fixed '%s' format strings are safe (no CWE-134).
getusershell()/endusershell() and DENY_SHELL logic assumed to match documented libc behavior.
limitations: OSFC2 branch (line 38) tests `pr_pw->uflg.fg_lock != 1` — the field-validity flag — rather than the lock value fd_lock; if fg_lock only marks fd_lock as valid, accounts actually locked via fd_lock would pass this check and proceed to password fetch (authorization gap). Dismissed only because the OSF/1 struct semantics cannot be quoted from this code; would be CWE-863 if confirmed on an OSFC2 build.

Passwordless accounts return RLM_MODULE_NOOP (lines 137-138) instead of REJECT (the FIXME acknowledges this); whether this lets the request be accepted depends on modules not shown, so the fail-open effect is not provable from this code.
pwd->pw_shell is used in strcmp (lines 75/88/96) without a NULL check; a NULL shell field from an NSS backend would crash there first — same CWE-476 class, weaker and conditional.

The NULL-password trigger requires the platform's passwd/shadow/NSS backend to actually return NULL (files-based glibc typically returns an empty string, not NULL); this environment-dependence is why confidence is not higher, but the code's own `encrypted_pass == NULL` test documents that NULL is a case this function was expected to handle.

verdict.summary: compand_drain indexes the delay buffer dbuf[dindex] with dindex seeded from s->delay_index and advanced by MOD(dindex + 1, s->delay_samples), but this code never validates that s->delay_frame is non-NULL, that s->delay_samples > 0, or that s->delay_index < s->delay_samples, and FFMIN(2048, s->delay_count) is used as the allocation size without any delay_count > 0 check. When the delay state is 0-sized or out of range (deriving from the public delay option and stream parameters, e.g. a delay that rounds to 0 at the active sample rate), the MOD wrap degenerates and dindex walks up to 2048 entries past the buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read whose contents are written into the output audio frame.

evidence.reason: Sink: dbuf[dindex] (line 22) is a heap read whose index is seeded from the unvalidated s->delay_index (line 20) and wrapped only by MOD(dindex + 1, s->delay_samples) (line 24). No check in this code enforces 0 <= delay_index < delay_samples, delay_samples > 0, or delay_frame non-NULL; with delay_samples == 0 or an at/out-of-range delay_index the index escapes the buffer for up to frame->nb_samples (<=2048) iterations, producing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125 rooted in CWE-129).

Origin of the faulty sizing/state: the drain length is taken as FFMIN(2048, s->delay_count) with no validation that s->delay_count > 0 or that it is consistent with s->delay_samples; this value becomes frame->nb_samples, the loop bound driving the unguarded dbuf[dindex] reads. The only quotable check (if (!frame)) covers allocation failure of the new frame, not the delay buffer state.

assumptions: MOD is an external macro; per the upstream FFmpeg source it is '#define MOD(a, b) (((a) >= (b)) ? (a) - (b) : (a))', which degenerates to the identity when b == 0 and only subtracts once.
Behavior of ff_get_audio_buffer/av_frame_get_buffer for non-positive nb_samples (likely rejection) is outside the given code and could not be quoted.

The write-side invariants (s->delay_index < s->delay_samples, s->delay_count <= initialized entries in the delay buffer) exist, if at all, only in code not shown; per guard-anchoring they are treated as absent.
Allocation sites and channel-count consistency of s->delay_frame and s->channels are not shown; C2 (NULL delay_frame) and C5 (channel mismatch) were not confirmed.
limitations: Candidates C2 (NULL dereference of s->delay_frame) and C5 (outlink->channels exceeding the s->channels / delay_frame plane count) could not be proven reachable from this fragment alone and are recorded only as assumptions.

C3 (uninitialized delay-buffer entries being drained into output) and C4 (non-positive nb_samples reaching allocation) depend on unshown write-side/framework behavior; they are subsumed into the confirmed missing-validation finding rather than reported as separate vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: In dxa_read_packet, the CMAP handler sets pal_size = 772 and reads the 768 palette bytes with avio_read(s->pb, pal + 4, 768) while discarding the return value, so on a short or failed read the tail of the stack buffer pal stays uninitialized. pal_size is never reduced, and the FRAM and NULL handlers then copy all 772 bytes into the output packet (memcpy(pkt->data, pal, pal_size)), leaking uninitialized stack memory in decoded output. Every other avio_read in the same function checks its return, but this one does not; no statement in the given code enforces full initialization.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: pal_size is set to 772 before the palette read, and the return value of avio_read(s->pb, pal + 4, 768) is ignored, so a short or failed read leaves pal[4..771] uninitialized while pal_size remains 772. Unlike lines 22 and 43, this avio_read is unchecked.

evidence.snippet: if(pal_size) memcpy(pkt->data, pal, pal_size);
evidence.reason: Sink (FRAM path): copies 772 bytes of the possibly partially uninitialized stack buffer pal into the output packet whenever a CMAP chunk with a short read was followed by a FRAM chunk, disclosing uninitialized stack contents.

evidence.snippet:
if(pal_size) memcpy(pkt->data, pal, pal_size);
    memcpy(pkt->data + pal_size, buf, 4);
evidence.reason: Sink (NULL path): same use of partially uninitialized pal bytes in packets emitted after a short CMAP read.

assumptions: DXA_EXTRA_SIZE is an unseen #define; the code's own AV_RB32(buf + 5) and avio_read(s->pb, buf + 4, DXA_EXTRA_SIZE - 4) imply it is at least 9.

c->frames, c->bytes_left, c->bpc, c->has_sound, c->wavpos, c->vidpos are produced by the demuxer header parser (dxa_read_header), which is not in the given code; their exact attainable ranges are unknown.

Whether a short avio_read always co-occurs with url_feof becoming true (which would end the loop) is an external FFmpeg internal behavior not quotable from this code; under the anchoring discipline it cannot be treated as an enforcing guard.
limitations: Sound-path candidate: FFMIN(c->bytes_left, c->bpc) mixes uint32_t and int, and the check 'if(ret != size)' compares int ret against unsigned size; if the header parser could yield c->bpc == -22 (AVERROR(EINVAL)) with bytes_left > 0xFFFFFFEA, the comparison would pass and return success with a non-allocated packet. Reachability depends on the unseen header parser and could not be concretely proven, so it is not counted as a confirmed finding.
A zero-length sound packet (c->bpc == 0) yields an empty but allocated packet; degradation only, no security effect.
The FRAM allocation arithmetic is safe: 'if(size > 0xFFFFFF)' bounds size, and size + DXA_EXTRA_SIZE + pal_size stays well below INT_MAX; all copies fit exactly within the allocation.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is provable in this code. Resolver-derived channel-arg values (lb policy name, addresses, service config JSON) cross a trust boundary, but every dangerous use is guarded in-code: the dangling-pointer hazard on lb_policy_name is prevented by gpr_strdup before grpc_channel_args_destroy, the log call is guarded by 'lb_policy_name != NULL', the addresses loop bound uses the same size_t unit, all ref/unref pairs (state_error, lb_policy, old_lb_policy, exit_idle, method_params_table, service_config_json) are balanced and NULL-guarded on every path, and mutex locking of info_mu is symmetric. Remaining candidates (assert-based aborts on resolver-arg types, GRPC_ERROR_NONE placed in error refs arrays, a one-shot closure-scheduling gap when LB policy creation fails while the resolver is alive) all require states or external-component behaviors that no statement in this code produces or that this code provably recovers from on the next resolver callback.

assumptions: chand->resolver_result and its channel args are constructed by resolver code outside this snippet; whether a resolver can emit a GRPC_ARG_LB_POLICY_NAME/GRPC_ARG_SERVICE_CONFIG arg with a non-string type or a mis-sized GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES array cannot be verified from the given code. The GPR_ASSERT type checks would abort on such data.

NUL-termination of channel_arg->value.string and correct allocation of addresses->addresses relative to addresses->num_addresses are invariants of the resolver, not enforced by statements in this code.

Behavior of external helpers gpr_strdup on NULL, grpc_service_config_create on malformed JSON, grpc_lb_policy_create on unknown names, GRPC_ERROR_CREATE_REFERENCING on refs entries equal to GRPC_ERROR_NONE, and grpc_lb_policy_check_connectivity's error output is not quotable here and was not relied upon for the verdict.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_STRING/GRPC_ARG_POINTER) aborts (potential DoS) if the resolver emits a wrong-typed arg; the resolver constructs these args internally, so the trigger is not reachable from data this code receives.

Candidate dismissed: 'grpc_error *refs[] = {error, state_error}' and GRPC_ERROR_CREATE_REFERENCING("Channel disconnected", &error, 1) can receive GRPC_ERROR_NONE if the else-branches are taken with error == GRPC_ERROR_NONE; reachability requires a NULL resolver with a NONE completion, a state this code does not produce, and the constructor's NONE-handling is external.

Candidate dismissed: when grpc_lb_policy_create fails (lb_policy == NULL) while chand->resolver != NULL, waiting_for_config_closures are neither scheduled nor failed in this invocation; the resolver is re-armed via grpc_resolver_next_locked on that same path, so the next resolver result re-enters this function and re-attempts scheduling — one-shot degradation, not a provable permanent stall.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table uses the caller-supplied, bitstream-derived ref_count[list] as the loop bound (line 27) with no validation against the capacity of the fixed-size pwt->luma_weight/pwt->chroma_weight arrays, and in the PICT_FRAME path writes to doubled indices 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1 (lines 71-76). Any ref_count whose expansion exceeds the array extent — reachable via num_ref_idx_active syntax on a weighted-prediction frame slice — produces attacker-influenced out-of-bounds writes of weight values (bounded to [-128,127] by the int8 check), corrupting memory adjacent to the H264PredWeightTable.

evidence.snippet:
pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i][list][0] = pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i + 1][list][0] = pwt->luma_weight[i][list][0];
                pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i][list][1] = pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i + 1][list][1] = pwt->luma_weight[i][list][1];
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: indices 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1 are computed from i, which is bounded only by the unvalidated external ref_count[list]; no statement in this code caps i or ref_count, so the write index grows without bound (already past a 32-entry table at i=8) whenever picture_structure == PICT_FRAME, corrupting memory past pwt->luma_weight (and identically pwt->chroma_weight at lines 75-76).

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < ref_count[list]; i++) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the unvalidated index: ref_count is an exported-API parameter derived from attacker-controlled num_ref_idx_active slice-header data and is used directly as the loop bound feeding every array write in the function, with no range check anywhere in this code — the missing validation site where the bound belongs.

assumptions: H264PredWeightTable's member arrays are fixed-size (their exact first-dimension capacity is not shown in the given code; upstream FFmpeg declares luma_weight/chroma_weight with a fixed first dimension of 32). For any fixed capacity, a sufficiently large ref_count crosses it; the given code itself demonstrates the required capacity is at least 2*ref_count+16 by writing index 16+2*i+1.

Upstream callers (h264_slice.c) parse num_ref_idx_active from the bitstream and are believed to permit ref_count up to 32; this bound is not quotable in the given code and was not relied upon for the verdict.
GetBitContext readers (get_ue_golomb/get_se_golomb/get_bits1) are assumed not to read past the bitstream buffer (framework guarantee, not present in this code).
pwt, sps, and ref_count are assumed non-NULL per caller contract; NULL would be a caller bug, not data-driven.
limitations: Weight values are stored into the tables (lines 31-32, 50-51) before the int8 range check (lines 33-34, 52-53); the function then returns AVERROR_INVALIDDATA. Only a caller that ignores the return value would consume the out-of-range values, so this was not counted as a vulnerability of this code.
Negative ref_count[list] values cause the inner loop to execute zero iterations; no defect.
The denom guards (luma/chroma_log2_weight_denom > 7U) were edge-tested, including sign-flipped/truncated get_ue_golomb results, and correctly reject all out-of-range values via unsigned promotion.

verdict.summary: The exported function hash_passwords uses the caller-supplied 'count' parameter directly as its loop bound and as the index into the 'passwords' vector without ever validating it against passwords.size(); any caller passing count > passwords.size() (or a negative count reaching result.reserve) causes out-of-bounds reads via passwords[i].c_str()/passwords[i].length() inside PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC, an attacker-reachable crash/DoS and potential OOB-data exposure. main itself constructs matching sizes, but hash_passwords is the documented public API entry point and must validate its own inputs.

evidence.snippet:
for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        // Create vectors for hash and salt
evidence.reason: Loop bound is the unvalidated public-API parameter 'count'; no statement in the function compares count to passwords.size(), so i can exceed the vector's extent.

Sink: passwords[i] is std::vector::operator[] with attacker-controlled index i bounded only by 'count' (line 23). Trigger: hash_passwords(count=3, ..., passwords with size 1) -> at i=1 an out-of-bounds vector element is read, then .c_str()/.length() dereference OOB heap memory passed to PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC; minimal fix (reject if count < 0 || (size_t)count > passwords.size()) is absent from the code.

assumptions: OpenSSL semantics: RAND_bytes returns 1 on success, 0 on failure, -1 if the active RAND method does not support byte generation; PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC returns 1 on success.
std::vector::operator[] performs no bounds checking (UB on out-of-range index).
limitations: result.reserve(count) at line 21 converts a negative 'count' to a huge size_t, throwing an uncaught exception (terminate/DoS); same root cause as the confirmed finding (unvalidated count).

if (!RAND_bytes(...)) at line 29 fails to catch a -1 return (only 0 is caught); if triggered it would use the value-initialized all-zero salt, but reaching -1 requires a non-default RAND method configuration that no input to this code can induce.
'usernames' is accepted but never used, and with an even argc the trailing unmatched argument is silently dropped; both are behavioral issues with no memory-safety effect.
main's own argv indexing is safe for all argc >= 3: max index 2+2*(count-1) = argc-1 (odd argc) or argc-2 (even argc).

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability found. All writes use fixed indices (0/1) with a constant length (2); the send sink is reached only with outlen>0 and outpos<outlen (guarded by 'if (ibe->outlen == 0) { goto check_reset; }' on entry and by the outlen=2/outpos=0 assignment before 'goto send'); the backward 'goto send' edge is one-shot because 'ibe->send_reset = false;' is set before jumping; and completion resets outlen/outpos to 0 on every path ('ibe->outlen = 0; ibe->outpos = 0;'). The only theoretical defect — outpos exceeding outlen if qemu_chr_fe_write returned more bytes than requested — requires the callee to violate its documented contract, which is not a state any input crossing this code's boundaries can induce.

assumptions: Declarations of struct fields (outbuf size, types of outlen/outpos) are not in the given snippet; indices 0 and 1 are used with a fixed 2-byte message, so only a 2-byte buffer is required.

qemu_chr_fe_write is assumed to return a negative error code or a count between 0 and the requested length (len == outlen - outpos); this contract is not visible in the given code. If the callee could return > len, 'ibe->outpos += ret' would push outpos past outlen and the next 'outlen - outpos' would be negative, widening to a huge size_t at the send sink. No guard against this exists in the given code, but it is unreachable without callee contract violation.
The declaration and initialization of ibe, including that outbuf is at least large enough for outlen values set elsewhere, are outside the given code.
'ibe->chr', timer callbacks, and the chardev backend behavior (including persistent-error retry cadence) are framework components outside this code.
limitations: A persistently failing/full chardev backend causes the 10ms timer to be re-armed indefinitely ('timer_mod_ns(... + 10000000)'), a bounded-retry degradation handled by the QEMU framework, not attacker-inducible resource exhaustion within this code.
This function only transmits; the receive/parse paths for external IPMI data are not shown and were not analyzed.

verdict.summary: In jpc_pi_nextrpcl, the packet-precinct index pi->prcno is computed from attacker-controlled JPEG-2000 codestream geometry (prcvind * numhprcs + prchind) and used to index pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos with no runtime bounds check — the only accompanying statement is `assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs);`, which is compiled out in release builds, checks only the upper bound (prcno may be negative via int overflow), and provides no rejection path. This yields a heap out-of-bounds read and write (`++(*prclyrno)`). Additionally, the overflow guard for the xstep/ystep shift computations tests `pi->picomp->numrlvls` while the shifts use the loop's `picomp->numrlvls`, so a component with a large numrlvls can produce shift counts >= 32 (undefined behavior) that the guard never rejects, and the resulting garbage values flow into the rpx/rpy shifts and the prcno computation.

evidence.reason: pi->prcno is derived entirely from attacker-controlled codestream values (image extents, hsamp/vsamp, prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn, numhprcs) at line 81, then used at line 87 to index the heap array prclyrnos and written through at line 89. The only guard is `assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs);`, which is a debug-only assertion (absent under NDEBUG), checks no lower bound (the int expression prcvind * numhprcs + prchind can overflow negative), and never returns an error. A crafted codestream with precinct geometry inconsistent with numhprcs/numprcs makes prcno >= numprcs, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (line 88) and out-of-bounds increment/write (line 89). Root cause: improper validation of array index (CWE-129).

The overflow guard checks `pi->picomp->numrlvls` (a stale pointer member that is not updated in this loop) while the shift counts at lines 36-39 use the current loop component's `picomp->numrlvls`. The guard therefore validates a different variable than the one shifted. With component 0 having a small numrlvls and another component (e.g., via a COC marker) having a large numrlvls plus a large prcwidthexpn, the guard passes (e.g., 20 + 1 = 21 <= 30) while the actual shift count is prcwidthexpn + numrlvls - rlvlno - 1 >= 32 — undefined shift behavior producing garbage xstep/ystep, which then propagate into rpx/rpy shifts (lines 65-74) and the unguarded prcno computation. Root cause: integer/shift overflow via a check on the wrong variable (CWE-190).

assumptions: pi->picomp is assumed to be initialized by the decoder (outside this code, e.g., to &pi->picomps[0]) before the first invocation; if it were NULL, the guard at lines 30-33 would itself be a NULL dereference.
JAS_UINTFAST32_NUMBITS is assumed to be 32 (the width of uint_fast32_t); the guard arithmetic in the given code depends on it.
assert is assumed to be disabled in release builds (NDEBUG), as is standard; with asserts active the prcno defect degrades to an assertion abort (denial of service) instead of memory corruption.
hsamp/vsamp are assumed to be constrained to nonzero values and numrlvls >= 1 by decoder-side validation not shown in this code; no such enforcement is quotable here.
limitations: Potential division by zero at `pi->ystep - (pi->y % pi->ystep)` / `pi->xstep - (pi->x % pi->xstep)` (lines 49-52) if every component has numrlvls == 0 or hsamp/vsamp == 0; reachability could not be proven from this code alone because the decoder's validation of those fields is not shown, and no guard exists in this function.

`pi->picomp = &pi->picomps[pi->compno]` executes before the loop condition is tested, so a pchg->compnostart >= pi->numcomps forms an out-of-bounds address; the loop condition `pi->compno < ... pi->numcomps` prevents any dereference, so this is UB without a memory-safety effect.
The goto skip into the innermost loop is an intentional resume mechanism; stale pi->lyrno is re-tested by the loop condition, so no additional defect was identified there.

verdict.summary: compand_drain allocates the output frame with exactly FFMIN(2048, s->delay_count) samples, so the drain loop reads at most the number of pending buffered samples (the fix for the historical af_compand uninitialized-read bug, which used delay_samples instead of delay_count). Allocation failure is NULL-checked (fail-closed), delay_count cannot underflow because frame->nb_samples <= delay_count by the same FFMIN clamp, channels is asserted positive before plane indexing, and the frame planes are allocated from the same outlink that supplies the loop's channel bound. No memory-safety, boundary, or fail-open defect is reachable from values this code receives.

assumptions: MOD(a,b) is the FFmpeg compand macro '#define MOD(a,b) (((a) >= (b) ? (a) - (b) : (a)))', which maps a valid ring index to a valid ring index; it is not defined in the given snippet.
s->delay_frame is allocated elsewhere with at least s->delay_samples doubles per channel, and s->channels has one ChanParam per channel; both sized at filter configuration time outside this snippet.

s->delay_index lies in [0, s->delay_samples) and s->delay_count >= 0 on entry, maintained by the filter's frame-processing and activation code outside this snippet; this function preserves both invariants (nb_samples <= delay_count, MOD-bounded index).
compand_drain is an internal filter callback invoked by the filter's activate/flush logic, not an intake point for external data; the state it consumes is produced by the same filter.
outlink->channels matches the channel count of s->delay_frame and s->channels via filter-graph format negotiation.
limitations: Dismissed C1 (uninitialized read of dbuf[dindex] when fewer samples were buffered than the ring size): the guard 'frame = ff_get_audio_buffer(outlink, FFMIN(2048, s->delay_count));' ties the read count to the pending-sample count, which is the upstream fix for this exact bug; without that line the defect would be real (CWE-908).
Dismissed C2 (out-of-range initial s->delay_index causing OOB read of dbuf): no reachable trigger inside this code; would require corrupted external state not producible here.
Dismissed C4 (delay_count <= 0 yielding non-positive nb_samples): allocation failure is NULL-checked and returns AVERROR(ENOMEM) (fail-closed); a zero-sample frame results in zero loop iterations.
Analysis is limited to the given snippet; the surrounding af_compand filter code (filter_frame, activate, uninit) was not provided and its invariants were treated as assumptions, not quoted guards.

verdict.summary: bdrv_write_compressed validates every caller-controlled sector-range parameter against a request check that is present on every path to both sinks: 'if (bdrv_check_request(bs, sector_num, nb_sectors)) return -EIO;' precedes both set_dirty_bitmap (line 12) and the driver dispatch (line 14), with no bypass branch, and drv is NULL-checked before dereference. The function performs no arithmetic, copying, or indexing of its own; it is a validated pass-through. Residual risk: the body of bdrv_check_request is not part of the given code, so its rejection of boundary values (nb_sectors = -1/INT_MAX, sector_num + nb_sectors overflow) cannot be audited from this snippet and is recorded as an assumption; a NULL bs parameter would crash at line 4 but is not producible from trust-boundary data.

assumptions: bdrv_check_request(bs, sector_num, nb_sectors) is assumed to return nonzero for invalid requests (negative nb_sectors or sector_num, sector_num + nb_sectors exceeding the device size, overflow at the int64 boundary). Its implementation is not included in the given code, so this bound could not be quoted or edge-tested; the call site itself is the quotable enforcement statement.
set_dirty_bitmap and the format driver's bdrv_write_compressed are assumed to be memory-safe for the validated (sector_num, nb_sectors) range; their bodies are outside this snippet.
Callers are assumed to pass a non-NULL BlockDriverState, matching the block-layer API contract.
limitations: No NULL check on the bs parameter: 'BlockDriver *drv = bs->drv;' dereferences bs unconditionally; a NULL bs would crash, but no trust-boundary data can make bs NULL through any in-tree caller, so this is hardening, not an attacker-reachable DoS.

If bdrv_check_request internally short-circuits for growable or unchecked images (a pattern present in some historical QEMU versions), negative or overflowing sector ranges would reach set_dirty_bitmap (bitmap word/bit indexing) and the driver write (nb_sectors * 512-byte read of buf); this cannot be confirmed or refuted from the given code alone.
set_dirty_bitmap is called before the write result is known; marking sectors dirty on a failed write is conservative/fail-safe with no security effect.
bs->drv and bs->dirty_tracking are read without locking; concurrent removability races are a framework-wide concern, not introduced by this function, and no interleaved mutation occurs within it.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety, bounds, injection, or authz defect is provable from this code alone. All sinks that consume attacker-influenced package data (fdata[fx] indexing, fsmFsPath/fsmSymlink/fsmMkfifo/fsmMknod path arguments, xcalloc(fc,...) sizing) are governed by contracts (rpmfiNext index range, header/path sanitization, enum stage ordering) that are not quotable within the given snippet; every check that IS present ((fx = rpmfiNext(fi)) >= 0, if (di.dirfd == -1), fx != RPMERR_ITER_END, the unknown-filetype else branch) edge-tests correctly at 0, -1, empty, and exactly-at-limit values. The unguarded upper index bound fx < fc and the FA_TOUCH 'continue' skipping fp->stage = FILE_UNPACK are recorded as limitations because their triggers are not constructible from this code.

assumptions: rpmfiNext(fi) returns an index in [0, rpmfilesFC(files)) for every iterator constructed from `files` in this function (rpmfilesIter / rpmfiNewArchiveReader with the same `files` object); this is the contract that keeps &fdata[fx] in bounds, and it is NOT quotable from the given code.
Package header validation (file-path canonicalization, '..' rejection, count limits) is performed in the rpmfiles/header layer before this function; no sanitization statement exists in this snippet.
xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata)) with fc == 0 yields a harmless non-NULL minimal allocation (rpm allocator behavior) and aborts the process on allocation failure; not quotable here.
fsmFsPath never returns NULL for processed entries, so fp->fpath passed to xstrdup at `*failedFile = xstrdup(fp->fpath)` is non-NULL; not quotable here.
Fclose(payload) tolerates a NULL payload handle; not quotable here.

The enum values FILE_NONE/FILE_PRE/FILE_UNPACK/FILE_PREP/FILE_COMMIT and their numeric ordering are defined outside the given code; the erase-pass condition `fp->stage > FILE_NONE` cannot be evaluated without them.
failedFile is non-NULL per the documented caller contract of this internal rpm API.
limitations: Candidate CWE-129 (fdata[fx] with no in-function upper bound against fc): the loop conditions only enforce `>= 0` verbatim; no `fx < fc` check exists in the snippet. Dismissed only because no concrete input can be constructed from the given code that makes rpmfiNext return fx >= fc; if the iterator contract were violated elsewhere, this would be a heap over-read.

Candidate (rollback file deletion): `if (fp->action == FA_TOUCH) continue;` provably skips `fp->stage = FILE_UNPACK;`, leaving stage at FILE_PRE from the first loop; the erase pass `if (rc && fp->stage > FILE_NONE && !fp->skip) (void) fsmRemove(fp->fpath, fp->sb.st_mode);` could then remove merely-touched pre-existing files on install failure. Trigger's final step depends on the FILE_* enum ordering, which is not in the given code.

Candidate (hardlink content misrouting): `else if (firstlink && rpmfiArchiveHasContent(fi))` lacks a check that the skipped file belongs to firstlink's hardlink set; content of one set could be written to a different set's file. Depends on rpmfiArchiveHasContent/fsmMkfile semantics not shown.

Candidate CWE-400: xcalloc(fc, ...) sizes memory from the header-controlled file count; allocation is linear in declared content with no amplification in this code, so dismissed as proportional resource use.

Candidate CWE-362 (TOCTOU between fsmVerify/fsmStat and the subsequent create calls): any O_EXCL/temp-suffix mitigation lives inside the fsm* helpers, not quotable here; the generic install-time race is a known rpm-wide design consideration, not a defect provable in this snippet.

verdict.summary: hfile_mem_get_buffer computes the buffer length with reversed pointer operands: '*length = file->buffer - file->limit;' (start - end). For any nonempty memory file this yields a negative ptrdiff_t that wraps to a huge value (~SIZE_MAX) when stored into the caller's size_t. The only guard, the backend check, does not constrain this arithmetic. Callers consuming the returned buffer/length pair perform massively out-of-bounds reads (crash/DoS, potential disclosure).

evidence.snippet:
if (length)
        *length = file->buffer - file->limit;
evidence.reason: The length written to the caller's size_t is computed as 'file->buffer - file->limit' (start minus end). For a memory-backend hFILE over any nonempty blob (buffer = data start, limit = data end), this is negative; conversion to size_t wraps to 2^64 - sz, a bogus huge length returned to callers who use it as a byte count for the returned buffer, causing out-of-bounds reads. No statement in the code corrects the operand order or bounds the result; the correct form 'file->limit - file->buffer' appears nowhere.

assumptions: The hFILE struct field semantics (buffer = start of the memory region, limit = end) come from the htslib hFILE/mem-backend layout, which is not included in the given snippet; the invariant buffer <= limit cannot be quoted from the given code and is recorded as an assumption.

It is assumed callers of this public API use the returned (buffer, length) pair for memory operations (reads/copies), which is the documented purpose of hfile_mem_get_buffer; the defect is the corrupted length produced regardless of caller behavior.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: file is dereferenced at 'if (file->backend != &mem_backend)' without a NULL check (CWE-476). Rejected because a NULL hFILE requires a caller programming error, not data crossing a trust boundary; no attacker-influenced value can make file NULL at this point.
The 'length' output pointer is guarded by 'if (length)' before the write; that check is present and passes the edge test for NULL.

verdict.summary: The command-line front end copies unbounded trust-boundary strings into fixed 255-byte stack buffers with strcpy (argv[optind] into aacFileName; optarg into audioFileName/adtsFileName) and parses option arguments with sscanf("%s") into char dr[10] with no width specifier, producing attacker-triggerable stack buffer overflows. Additionally the 8-byte fread into the uninitialized header[] array has its return value unchecked, so a file shorter than 8 bytes causes uninitialized stack bytes to control the mp4-vs-AAC branch.

evidence.snippet:
/* point to the specified file name */
    strcpy(aacFileName, argv[optind]);
evidence.reason: Unbounded strcpy of the first non-option CLI argument (attacker-controlled string of arbitrary length) into char aacFileName[255] declared at the top of main. The only prior guard, 'if (((argc - optind) < 1) || showHelp)', verifies argument count, not length; no length check exists on any path. Trigger: a filename of >= 255 bytes overflows the stack array past its end.

The -o option's argument is copied with strcpy into char audioFileName[255]; the only guard is the NULL check 'if (optarg)'. Any -o argument longer than 254 bytes overflows the stack buffer. The -a handler (strcpy(adtsFileName, optarg)) has the identical defect.

sscanf with the unbounded "%s" conversion writes into char dr[10]; an option argument of 10 or more non-whitespace characters (e.g. -s AAAAAAAAAA) writes past the 10-byte stack buffer. The same pattern repeats in the -f, -b, and -l handlers. Any subsequent atoi range checks occur after the overflow and check a different quantity.

The return value of fread is not checked, and header is an uninitialized automatic array. A file shorter than 8 bytes (edge case: 0-byte or 7-byte file) leaves header[4..7] uninitialized; those values then decide the mp4file branch and are pushed back via ungetc in the stdin path — attacker-influenced use of uninitialized memory (CWE-457).

assumptions: getopt_long is assumed to populate optarg as a NUL-terminated string for options taking arguments (the optstring "o:a:s:f:b:l:wgdhitq" marks o,a,s,f,b,l as requiring arguments).
argv[0] (assigned to progName at 'progName = argv[0];') is assumed non-NULL per normal process invocation; the argc==0 exotic-exec case is not treated as reachable.
decodeMP4file/decodeAACfile internals are not shown; their handling of the file contents is out of scope for this analysis.

file_ext[] is an external table assumed to have at least 3 entries so file_ext[format] with format in {1,2} is in range (format is constrained by 'if ((format < 1) || (format > 2)) showHelp = 1;' plus the early exit).
limitations: The float division length/dec_length at the final fprintf can divide by zero only if the decode completes within one clock tick; IEEE floating-point division yields inf rather than a crash, so no vulnerability is recorded.

strcat(audioFileName, file_ext[format]) at the output-name construction can extend past 255 bytes, but only after the unbounded strcpy of the same root cause has already overflowed; it is covered by the primary CWE-120 finding rather than listed separately.
progName = argv[0] could be NULL only if the process were exec'd with an empty argv vector, an environment condition not inducible by this program's normal inputs.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset allocates the guest response with non-zeroing g_malloc, initializes only resp->hdr.type, and transmits sizeof(*resp) + max_size bytes to the guest, disclosing uninitialized host heap memory (hdr.flags, hdr.fence_id, hdr.ctx_id, padding, and any capset_data bytes virgl_renderer_fill_caps does not write, since the buffer was sized from max_size while fill_caps writes per the attacker-chosen capset_version). The only guard, `if (!max_size)`, rejects only the zero case and does nothing to enforce initialization.

evidence.reason: The response buffer is allocated with non-zeroing g_malloc (line 14) and only hdr.type is initialized (line 15); no memset/g_malloc0 exists anywhere in the function. virtio_gpu_ctrl_response (line 19) is passed the full length sizeof(*resp) + max_size, so uninitialized heap bytes (hdr.flags/fence_id/ctx_id/padding, plus capset_data tail bytes not written by virgl_renderer_fill_caps when the guest-requested gc.capset_version is smaller than the max version the size was computed for) are transmitted to the guest. Trigger: guest sends GET_CAPSET with any capset_id for which max_size != 0 (the line-10 guard rejects only the value 0).

assumptions: virgl_renderer_get_cap_set is assumed to always write to *max_ver/*max_size (including returning 0 for unknown capset_id) — the `if (!max_size)` guard suggests the author relied on this, but it is enforced outside the given code; otherwise max_size itself would be an uninitialized read (CWE-457) at line 14.
virtio_gpu_ctrl_response is assumed to transmit resp_len bytes starting at &resp->hdr, as implied by passing sizeof(*resp) + max_size; its implementation is outside the given code.

virgl_renderer_fill_caps is assumed not to write more than max_size bytes; if it does (e.g., for an unvalidated gc.capset_version, which is never checked against max_ver), a heap buffer overflow would additionally exist — unprovable from the given snippet.

Host is assumed 64-bit; on a 32-bit host, sizeof(*resp) + max_size could wrap in size_t if the renderer ever returned a value near UINT32_MAX for a guest-selected capset_id — no upper bound on max_size exists in this code (the guard rejects only 0).
limitations: max_ver is computed but never used; gc.capset_version is passed unvalidated to virgl_renderer_fill_caps. Whether this causes an out-of-bounds write depends on the external virglrenderer library and cannot be proven from the given code alone.

A hostile/garbage max_size from the renderer (huge values, or unset values on error paths) would turn the g_malloc into a wrap or abort, but nothing in the given code shows a reachable input producing such a value.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-influenced input is the logout request parameter 'url'. Every path to the redirect sink is guarded: NULL/empty values are replaced by the trusted configured default (c->default_slo_url), and any non-empty value must pass oidc_validate_post_logout_url, whose failure returns HTTP_BAD_REQUEST before the value is used to build the logout request or is passed to the final handler. Both interpolations into the end-session URL (id_token_hint and url) are wrapped in oidc_util_escape_string, preventing query-string injection. The NULL-dereference edge case at apr_strnatcmp(url, "") is prevented by the short-circuit (url == NULL) || in the same condition. No candidate survived the counterfactual patch test.

assumptions: The bodies of oidc_validate_post_logout_url, oidc_is_front_channel_logout, oidc_is_back_channel_logout, oidc_handle_logout_request, oidc_handle_logout_backchannel, and oidc_util_escape_string are not included in the given code; this analysis relies on the observable call sites: validation failure returns HTTP_BAD_REQUEST (fail-closed) and escaping is applied at both interpolations.
c->default_slo_url and provider->end_session_endpoint are administrator/provider configuration treated as trusted, not attacker-controlled.
session-derived id_token_hint originates from the provider; it is escaped before interpolation, and the code path using it is guarded by 'if (id_token_hint != NULL)'.
limitations: oidc_debug(r, "enter (url=%s)", url) logs the raw attacker-controlled parameter; a value containing line breaks could forge log entries (CWE-117). This is treated as a debug-build-only concern since the oidc_debug facility in this module is a compiled-out no-op in production builds; if it were an unconditional production log line it would be a low-severity log-forging finding.
Whether oidc_validate_post_logout_url itself has a flawed allow-list cannot be judged from the given code; if that helper is weak, the root cause would live in the helper, not in this function.

verdict.summary: The logout redirect URL taken from the request parameter post_logout_redirect_uri is validated only if apr_uri_parse yields a non-NULL hostname: the guard '(uri.hostname != NULL) && ((strstr(c_host, uri.hostname) == NULL) || (strstr(uri.hostname, c_host) == NULL))' is skipped entirely for URLs with no parseable host, such as the protocol-relative URL '//evil.com/' or scheme-relative 'https:evil.com'. Such values pass the parse and CR/LF checks and reach the logout redirect sink ('return oidc_handle_logout_request(r, c, session, url)') or are embedded as post_logout_redirect_uri, giving an attacker an open redirect / attacker-controlled post-logout destination.

evidence.reason: The same-origin hostname guard is gated on 'uri.hostname != NULL': when the attacker-supplied logout URL parses without a hostname (e.g. '//evil.com/' or 'https:evil.com'), the entire host check is skipped, so no statement constrains the redirect destination.

evidence.snippet: return oidc_handle_logout_request(r, c, session, url);
evidence.reason: Sink: the unvalidated attacker-controlled logout URL (only filtered by apr_uri_parse success, the bypassed hostname check, and the CR/LF check) is passed as the redirect target, enabling an open redirect to an attacker-chosen destination such as '//evil.com/'.

evidence.snippet: oidc_util_get_request_parameter(r, OIDC_REDIRECT_URI_REQUEST_LOGOUT, &url);
evidence.reason: Trust-boundary entry point: the logout URL originates as an unvalidated HTTP request parameter controlled by the attacker.

assumptions: oidc_handle_logout_request ultimately issues an HTTP redirect (Location header) to the url argument; its body is outside the given code, but that is the function's documented purpose.
oidc_is_front_channel_logout / oidc_is_back_channel_logout match only specific logout-command URL shapes and do not reject protocol-relative or non-http URLs; their bodies are not in the given code.
apr_uri_parse succeeds with uri.hostname == NULL for inputs such as '//evil.com/' or 'https:evil.com'; this is the standard behavior of APR's URI parser but could not be quoted from the given code.

oidc_util_html_send_error HTML-escapes error_description and oidc_error sanitizes log output; if not, the reflected/logged attacker URL (lines 29-31) would additionally yield XSS/log injection, which cannot be confirmed from the given code.
c->default_slo_url, provider metadata (end_session_endpoint), and session contents are trusted module-established state.
limitations: The case-sensitive strstr hostname comparison fails closed for non-identical host spellings; it causes spurious rejections (DoS of convenience) rather than a bypass.
The reflected error messages containing the raw attacker URL are only a vulnerability if the error helpers fail to sanitize; not confirmable in the given code.

The Host-header-derived c_host dependence could weaken the check in Host-header-attack scenarios, but exploiting it requires control of the victim's Host header (proxy/DNS rebinding), not reachable via the parameter alone.

verdict.summary: In _php_mb_regex_ereg_replace_exec, the replacement-template loop computes fwd = php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex(p, enc) from the lead byte alone (no length argument, so it cannot know the buffer end) and copies fwd bytes via out_buf.append(p, fwd) without checking i + fwd <= replacement.size(). If the attacker-supplied replacement string ends with a truncated multibyte lead byte (e.g. 0xF0 at the last byte under UTF-8, or 0x8F under EUC-JP), fwd exceeds the remaining byte count and up to maxlen-1 bytes past the end of the replacement's heap buffer are read and appended to the output returned by the function — an out-of-bounds read that leaks adjacent heap memory to the caller.

evidence.reason: Unguarded copy sink: fwd (attacker-controlled multibyte char length derived from the replacement's final lead byte) is used as the copy length with no check that i + fwd <= replacement.size(); when replacement ends with a truncated multibyte lead byte under a multibyte regex encoding, out_buf.append(p, fwd) reads past the end of the replacement buffer and the out-of-bounds bytes are returned to the caller at line 131 (information disclosure / CWE-125).

Origin of the faulty value: fwd is computed from the lead byte of the attacker-supplied replacement string (line 86) without any remaining-length bound; the only remaining-length check in the loop, '(replacement.size() - i) >= 2' (line 88), merely gates the two-byte backref syntax and never bounds fwd, so at i = replacement.size()-1 with a multibyte lead byte, fwd exceeds the one remaining byte and flows to the unguarded append at lines 100-104.

assumptions: php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex(p, enc) derives the character length from the lead byte(s) per the selected encoding and receives no buffer-length parameter, so it cannot clamp fwd to the remaining bytes; enc is a multibyte encoding whenever the script sets mb_regex_encoding to one (e.g. UTF-8), since enc is resolved from MBSTRG(current_mbctype) via mbfl_name2encoding.

The prefix copy at line 80 assumes onig_search invariants (a returned match satisfies beg[0] >= pos offset and beg[0] within [0, str.size()]); no equivalent explicit check exists in this code, but no counterexample path is constructible from the given code alone.
regs->beg[]/end[] values index str as produced by onig_search over [str.data(), string_lim); the backref copy is explicitly bounded by lines 92-94, so that sink is guarded.
HHVM String data buffers are sized to the string length (plus terminator), so bytes beyond replacement.size() lie outside the allocation.
limitations: Empty-match advance at end-of-string (lines 106-113) can make pos = string_lim+1 via 'pos++' if onig_search were to return an empty match with start == range == string_lim, after which line 64 passes start > end to onig_search; whether oniguruma can return such a match, and how it handles start > end, is an external-library property not quotable in this code, so this candidate is not confirmed. The append at line 117 remains guarded by 'if (string_lim - pos > 0)'.

Truncation of the 64-bit OnigPosition regs->end[0] into int n at line 106 only manifests for subject strings larger than 2GB and degrades to byte-at-a-time copying that still terminates; not confirmed as a vulnerability.
The 'e' (eval) replacement option is neutralized verbatim by 'if (eval) { throw_not_supported("ereg_replace", "dynamic coding"); }' before use, so no code-execution finding arises.
The non-string pattern path (pat_buf, lines 42-45) writes only indices 0 and 1 of 'char pat_buf[2]' and is in-bounds.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table uses the attacker-influenced, unvalidated ref_count[list] as its only loop bound (line 26) and, when picture_structure == PICT_FRAME, writes mirrored weights at indices 16 + 2*i and 16 + 2*i + 1 (lines 69-74). The code's own indexing design covers at most i = 15 (max index 47), yet no statement anywhere bounds ref_count[list] <= 16 (or <= array size), so ref_count > 16 with PICT_FRAME — or a large ref_count in any mode — produces out-of-bounds writes of bitstream-controlled values into pwt->luma_weight/pwt->chroma_weight (CWE-129). Additionally, pwt->chroma_log2_weight_denom is assigned only under 'if (sps->chroma_format_idc)' yet read unconditionally at lines 17-22, so with a monochrome SPS the function reads an uninitialized/stale field into a comparison and an av_log %d message, and lines 73-74 copy never-written chroma_weight slots (CWE-908).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds sink: the frame-mode doubling writes index luma_weight/chroma_weight at 16 + 2*i and 16 + 2*i + 1, whose design maximum (i = 15) is index 47. The only bound on i is the caller-supplied 'ref_count[list]' loop condition on line 26; the function contains no check that ref_count[list] <= 16 when picture_structure == PICT_FRAME (or any absolute array bound). Trigger: chroma_format_idc = 1, denoms <= 7, slice_type_nos = P, picture_structure = PICT_FRAME, ref_count[0] = 17 (a value a caller of this exported function may pass; it derives from the bitstream's num_ref_idx_active_minus1 + 1, which the spec permits up to 32) — at i = 16 the code writes indices 48/49, one-past the design extent, with attacker-chosen int8-bounded weight values (CWE-129).

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < ref_count[list]; i++) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value and the missing-check site: ref_count[list] is an attacker-influenced parameter (derived from the parsed slice header) consumed here as the sole loop bound feeding every array index in the function. No statement in this code compares ref_count[list] against 16, 32, or the weight-array dimension; picture_structure is used only as the PICT_FRAME gate at line 69, never as a bound on ref_count, so the loop can run i past the array extent (CWE-129).

evidence.snippet:
if (sps->chroma_format_idc)
        pwt->chroma_log2_weight_denom = get_ue_golomb(gb);
evidence.reason: Missing initialization: pwt->chroma_log2_weight_denom is assigned only when sps->chroma_format_idc is nonzero, but it is read unconditionally at lines 17-22 (the '> 7U' comparison, the av_log %d message, and the '1 <<' shift operand). With a monochrome SPS (chroma_format_idc == 0) on the first call, this code reads a field it never wrote and can leak the uninitialized value into the error log; likewise, lines 73-74 copy pwt->chroma_weight[i][list][j][*] slots that no path wrote when chroma_format_idc == 0 (CWE-908).

assumptions: The definition of H264PredWeightTable is not included in the given code; based on the code's own indexing scheme (direct slots 0..15 plus mirrored slots 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1, design maximum index 16+2*15+1 = 47) and FFmpeg's h264_parse.h, the luma_weight/chroma_weight first dimension is assumed to be 48. Under that assumption any i > 15 in frame mode, or any i >= 48 in any mode, writes out of bounds; if the dimension were smaller the defect is strictly worse.
get_ue_golomb, get_se_golomb, and get_bits1 (GetBitContext) are assumed to handle bitstream exhaustion internally; their implementations are outside the given code.

ref_count is assumed to derive from the H.264 bitstream field num_ref_idx_active_minus1 (+1) parsed by the caller, per this function's role as the exported weighted-prediction parser; per the analysis rules the unquoted caller cannot be credited with bounding it.
PICT_FRAME and AV_PICTURE_TYPE_B are assumed to have their standard FFmpeg values.
limitations: In the upstream FFmpeg deployment the caller (decode_slice_header) performs a max-refs check on ref_count; that statement is not present in the given code and therefore cannot be credited under guard anchoring — within this code the bound does not exist.
Integer overflow of '16 + 2 * i' (candidate C) was subsumed by the ref_count finding: it is reachable only through the same unbounded loop bound.

The CWE-908 finding's worst effect is an uninitialized read feeding a comparison and a log line and propagation of stale/unwritten chroma slots; the '> 7U' clamp does bound the subsequent shift operand to 0..7, so it is a low-severity secondary finding.

verdict.summary: nfs3svc_decode_writeargs performs the three 32-bit loads of count/stable/len (and the prior decode_fh/xdr_decode_hyper advances) before the only bounds check against head->iov_base + head->iov_len, so a truncated WRITE request causes out-of-bounds reads past the head buffer (check-after-use). Additionally, the received-length guard `if (dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4)` wraps for len >= 0xFFFFFFFD (XDR_QUADLEN(len) = ((len+3)>>2) overflows), so count == len == 0xFFFFFFFF passes vacuously; the subsequent clamp sets len = max_blocksize, which may exceed the data actually received, and the unbounded page-walk loop then indexes rq_pages beyond the pages populated for this request, leading to NULL/stale page dereference and later copying of unvalidated data.

evidence.reason: Check-after-use out-of-bounds read: the three *p++ loads dereference p before the only bounds check (line 17) executes. A WRITE request truncated so that fewer than 12 bytes remain in the head buffer after the offset field (or one whose decode_fh/xdr_decode_hyper advance already pushed p past head->iov_base+head->iov_len, since nothing bounds p between lines 9 and 14) makes lines 14-16 read up to 12 bytes past the received buffer; the check then returns 0 only after the OOB reads occurred.

evidence.snippet: len = args->len = ntohl(*p++);
evidence.reason: Origin of the attacker-controlled 32-bit len that later reaches the wrapped guard at line 39 and the page-walk loop at lines 49-53; it is bounded by nothing except the (wrappable) dlen check and the max_blocksize clamp.

Unsigned wrap inside the guard's own arithmetic: XDR_QUADLEN(len) = ((len+3)>>2), so for len = 0xFFFFFFFF (count == len passes the equality check at line 22) len+3 wraps to 2, the product is 0, and dlen < 0 never holds, so the received-length invariant is never established. The clamp then sets len = max_blocksize, which may exceed the bytes actually received; no later statement re-validates len against dlen.

Unbounded sink reached by the wrapped len: when len exceeds the data actually received (e.g., after the line-39 wrap bypass plus the max_blocksize clamp, or when dlen is satisfied only by tail bytes that this loop never maps), v walks past the pages populated for this request and page_address(rqstp->rq_pages[v]) is computed on unallocated/stale entries; the resulting vectors describe count bytes never validated as received, which the WRITE handler later copies.

assumptions: decode_fh and xdr_decode_hyper internals are not shown in the given code; they are treated as unchecked sequential readers advancing p by attacker-chosen amounts (nothing in the given code bounds p between lines 9 and 14).

The state of rqstp->rq_pages entries beyond the pages populated for the current request (NULL vs. stale pointers from a pooled svc_rqst) is determined by the sunrpc layer, not by this code; either way the loop over-walk indices the array was never filled to for this request.
svc_max_payload(rqstp) is a trusted server/transport configuration value; its exact relation to the number of received pages is external to this code.
The head buffer backing head->iov_base and its allocation size (e.g., page-backed) are external facts; the OOB reads at lines 14-16 are established purely from the missing pre-read check.
Downstream nfsd3_proc_write consumes rq_vec/args->vlen/args->count per the function's contract; its copying behavior is outside the given code.
limitations: If head->iov_len is sufficiently smaller than the underlying head buffer allocation, the up-to-12-byte overread at lines 14-16 lands in uninitialized same-page bytes with no fault; the defect still stands because the loads precede any validation, and the p-advance from decode_fh can place them past the allocation.

Whether the page over-walk produces a NULL dereference, a stale-page use-after-free read, or disclosure via the subsequent file write depends on svc-layer page handling (see assumptions); the in-code root causes (check-after-use and the XDR_QUADLEN wrap) are independent of that.

The dlen computation counts tail->iov_len but the loop never maps tail bytes; exploiting that path alone requires a transport/GSS unwrap that populates tail with attacker-chosen length, which is environment-dependent.

verdict.summary: This calloc implementation correctly guards the allocation-size multiplication against size_t overflow: 'if (lb && n > GC_SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;' is the first statement of the function, so both allocation sinks (GC_malloc_uncollectable(n*lb) and REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb)) are reached only with a non-wrapping product, including at the boundary values n=0, lb=0, and n=GC_SIZE_MAX/lb exactly. No other attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, or validation defect is provable from the given code.

assumptions: GC_SIZE_MAX is assumed to be a size_t-domain constant equal to (or not exceeding) SIZE_MAX; if it were somehow defined for a wider type than size_t the guard could be unsound, but this definition is not present in the given code and a size_t constant cannot exceed SIZE_MAX.
The semantics of REDIRECT_MALLOC (whether it clears memory, and its own failure behavior) are not defined in the given code; the allocation primitive is treated as a black box.

GC_init_lib_bounds() is assumed to set GC_libpthread_start/end and GC_libld_start/end on failure to values (e.g., 0) that make the caller-range comparisons fail closed; its definition is outside this code.

verdict.summary: radare2 comment-command handler analyzed as its own intake point. The suspicious allocation 'text = malloc (strlen (comment) + strlen (newcomment) + 2);' whose copy uses 'nc' is exactly sufficient at the boundary: nc = strdup(newcomment) so strlen(nc) == strlen(newcomment), and r_str_unescape/r_str_ansi_strip only shrink, so strcpy(comment)+strcat(" ")+strcat(nc) writes exactly strlen(comment)+strlen(nc)+2 bytes == the allocation, a zero-slack exact fit with no overflow. Format strings are constants with attacker data only in %s/%x slots. r_num_math, r_meta_set/del/set_string/get_string, r_core_editor, and the r_meta_print_* helpers enforce their own parameter contracts; no bound on their behavior is claimed as a guard for any sink in this code.

The check is genuinely absent, but the replayed string is the same local user's own input executing with the user's existing r2 authority, so no trust boundary or capability is crossed.

If a future version of r_str_unescape or r_str_ansi_strip could expand the string, the '+' case allocation would become insufficient; under the semantics paired with this code the fit is exact, so no overflow exists in the analyzed version.

On 32-bit size_t builds, numSpecs = 0x20000000 yields 0x20000000 * 8 = 2^32, which wraps to 0, so the exact-size check passes for a 12-byte header-only request even though numSpecs remains 2^29; the handler then walks 2^29 spec entries out of the request buffer, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) rooted in the wrapping multiply (CWE-190).

The fragment at lines 12-15 is assumed to be the (redaction-damaged) initialization of ctx with the specs pointer and numSpecs; taken literally the statement is syntactically incomplete and the snippet does not compile as shown.

On 64-bit builds the CARD32 * size_t product is evaluated in 64-bit size_t and cannot wrap (max 0xFFFFFFFF*8 fits), so the wrapped-value trigger requires a 32-bit size_t build configuration, which the X server supports.
